title: Choosing a camp, and firewood

names.gloss: charcoal; hot coals or hot ashes

identification.basis: Anderson's account of where Kuku Yalanji people camped by season and which woods they burned, with the dictionary's fire and camp words and the station's camping rules.

summary: **[bayan](word:bayan)** is 'house, camp, shelter', **[baya](word:baya)** 'flame, fire' and 'firewood', **[kubu](word:kubu)** smoke, **[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)** 'charcoal; hot coals or hot ashes', **[nulu](word:nulu)** ashes, **[jakalambal](word:jakalambal)** 'start a fire, start to cook food', and **[balnji](word:balnji)**, 'doing something right', is the word for 'properly with a fire as in cooking or hardening spears over a fire' and also for 'camping out' [ref:hershberger1982]. 'Collecting firewood was usually women's work and different woods were used for different purposes. If conditions were rainy and damp, wood from the "kerosene tree" made an excellent fire starter. Inner portions of bark from the forest paper bark tree could also be used for this purpose. Dead branches from the grey boxwood (*Eucalyptus tessellaris*) made the best cooking wood: it is very hard, but splits easily and burns slowly and intensely. Some wood was very dangerous to use as firewood. For instance, a mangrove species, *Excoecaria agallocha*, produces a smoke which is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness. This is also true of the "brown cedar", *Canarium australasicum*' [ref:anderson1996].

infobox.label: Dry-season camp
infobox.value: Sandy creek beds and the sandy terraces above the running water; small family 'branch' camps out after eels, turtles, wallabies and goannas

infobox.label: Wet-season camp
infobox.value: The ridges between creek gullies, above flood level, near water; bigger camps

infobox.label: Firewood
infobox.value: Carbeen (Moreton Bay ash) dead branches for cooking; kerosene tree and paperbark inner bark for starting; never the milky mangrove or the brown cedar

infobox.label: Never camp
infobox.value: Under a river red gum's dead limbs; at the water's edge; in a creek bed in the wet; in long grass in the fire season

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[bayan](word:bayan)** 'house, camp, shelter'; **[warrbi](word:warrbi)** 'house made of grass, "beehive house"' (also 'axe'); **[kararr](word:kararr)** 'a blanket, sheet, or grass bedding spread out to lie on'; **[kakarr](word:kakarr)** 'grass; blanket to lie on, not to put over you'. **[baya](word:baya)** 'flame, fire; firewood', with 'baya wayu, light a fire'; **[jakalambal](word:jakalambal)** 'start a fire, start to cook food'; **[kubu](word:kubu)** 'smoke'; **[ngunjil](word:ngunjil)** 'charcoal; hot coals or hot ashes'; **[nulu](word:nulu)** 'ashes'; **[jidi](word:jidi)** 'paperbark tree bark torch'; **[balnji](word:balnji)** 'doing something right; properly with a fire as in cooking or hardening spears over a fire; camping out' [ref:hershberger1982]. The [huts and shelters](entry:huts-and-shelters) page has the words and the building of the shelters themselves, and the [firestick](entry:firestick) page the making of fire.

sections.heading: Where the old people camped, and what they burned
sections.body:
**The camps by season.** The camps moved with the year: in the dry, on the sand by the water; in the wet, up on the ridges above the flood. Each place has its own record above [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910-huts].

**Firewood.** 'Collecting firewood was usually women's work and different woods were used for different purposes. If conditions were rainy and damp, wood from the "kerosene tree" (*Halfordia scleroxyla*) made an excellent fire starter. Inner portions of bark from the forest paper bark tree (*Melaleuca leucadendron*) could also be used for this purpose. Dead branches from the grey boxwood (*Eucalyptus tessellaris*) made the best cooking wood: it is very hard, but splits easily and burns slowly and intensely. Some wood was very dangerous to use as firewood. For instance, a mangrove species, *Excoecaria agallocha*, produces a smoke which is said by Kuku-Yalanji to produce blindness. This is also true of the "brown cedar", *Canarium australasicum*' [ref:anderson1996]. The grey boxwood is the carbeen or Moreton Bay ash, the dictionary's *bajar*; the paperbark is the river's; the kerosene tree is a rainforest tree of the coast; the milky mangrove's inland cousin is the gutta-percha tree of the flood flats, whose sap is 'very dangerous to the eyes', and the [brown cedar](entry:brown-cedar) has its own page [ref:wiki-tessellaris] [ref:wiki-leucadendra] [ref:wiki-excoecaria] [ref:rfk-canarium]. The ironbark gum 'carried on a small stick in a man's bag with his firesticks' is on the [woodland](entry:woodland) page [ref:anderson1996].

**Roth's note on sleeping.** On the Bloomfield the huts were closed and smoked against the mosquitoes, and the [huts and shelters](entry:huts-and-shelters) page has the dome hut, the lean-to and the wet-season shelter from Roth's 1910 bulletin [ref:roth1910-huts]. The dictionary's **[kamu](word:kamu)** is the mosquito, and the dusk fire's **[kubu](word:kubu)** was the answer to it [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Good camp, bad camp
sections.body:
- **Good in the dry**: a sandy terrace above the pool, shade from paperbarks, a breeze, a view of the water, the fire on sand [ref:anderson1996].
- **Good in the wet**: a ridge between gullies, above any flood mark, with the water a short walk down [ref:anderson1996].
- **Bad**: under a [river red gum](entry:river-red-gum) with dead limbs, which 'often fall without warning' [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Bad**: on the water's edge or on a crocodile slide; camp back from the water and fill from a clear bank [ref:crocwise].
- **Bad**: in a creek bed with the build-up storms about; the dry creek is the dry-season camp only [ref:anderson1996].
- **Bad**: in long grass in the late dry, downwind of a burn; see [hunting with fire](entry:hunting-with-fire) [ref:pbg-cape-york].
- **Bad**: under a tree with termite mud tubes up it; see [termites](entry:termites-and-ant-beds) [ref:wiki-mastotermes].

sections.heading: Reading an old camp
sections.body:
- **Mussel shell heaps and charcoal** on a sandy terrace: the old dry-season camp; see [mussels](entry:mussels).
- **Grinding hollows** in a flat rock by a fast riffle, the dictionary's *jinali*: a zamia-processing camp [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Flood debris in the trees** above the terrace: how high the wet comes, and why the wet camp is on the ridge [ref:anderson1996].
- **A scarred tree** where bark was taken for a hut or a trough; see [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs).
- **Split dead branches of carbeen** under a tree: the cooking wood [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: The camp country
sections.body: The sandy terraces and creek beds in the dry, the ridges above them in the wet, and the big dry-season camps at the food-processing places [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: The camp in the country
sections.body: A camp is where the country's food comes together, and everything that eats comes to it: the [crows, magpies and butcherbirds](entry:bush-birds), the [kookaburra](entry:kookaburras-and-kingfishers) at the table, the [quoll](entry:quolls-bandicoots-and-rats) and the [possum](entry:possums) at night, the [dingo](entry:dingo-and-dogs) at the edge, the [pigs](entry:pigs) at the rubbish, the [goanna](entry:goanna) in the bins, the mosquitoes at dusk, and the crocodile at the place the fish are cleaned [ref:wiki-brushtail] [ref:crocwise]. The old people's answer was to move: short shifts along the creek, branch camps in the dry, the big camp when the zamia was in [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Dry: the creek-bed and terrace camps and the branch camps; wet: the ridge camps and the big shelters; the build-up: the move up before the storms [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Firewood by job
sections.body:
- **Starting**: kerosene-tree wood in the wet, paperbark inner bark, a paperbark torch, *jidi* [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Cooking**: carbeen dead branches, 'very hard, but splits easily and burns slowly and intensely'; the ironbarks and river red gum for long coals [ref:anderson1996] [ref:wiki-camaldulensis].
- **Smoke** against mosquitoes: a green or punky log on the dusk fire [ref:hershberger1982].
- **The earth oven**: see [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) and [cooking meat](entry:cooking-meat) [ref:roth1901].
- **Never**: the milky mangrove, the gutta-percha, the brown cedar, whose smoke blinds, and the poison nut, whose smoke 'is poisonous when roasting the nut' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Making a camp on the river
sections.body:
1. **Pick the terrace, not the beach**: a sandy bench above the pool with shade, a breeze, and a view of the water; in the build-up, pick the ridge [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Look up**: no dead limbs, no hollow red gum, no termite tubes over the swags [ref:wiki-camaldulensis] [ref:wiki-mastotermes].
3. **Look down**: the flood-line in the trees and the crocodile slides on the bank; be well above the one and well away from the other [ref:anderson1996] [ref:crocwise].
4. **Set the fire on sand**, clear the grass round it, and gather the cooking wood from the dead carbeen, box and gum branches on the ground; keep the starter bark dry [ref:anderson1996].
5. **Know the smoke**: no milky-sapped wood on the fire [ref:anderson1996].
6. **Water and fish-cleaning** at a different place from the swimming and the camp, never the same spot twice [ref:crocwise].
7. **Food up and closed** against the quoll, the possum, the crow and the pig; rubbish out, not buried by the water.
8. **Smoke at dusk** and the net at night; the mosquito is the one animal here that will make you sick for months; see [bites and stings](entry:bites-and-stings) [ref:healthdirect-ross-river].
9. **Follow the rules of the place**: the landholder's or the park's, and the Traditional Owners'. Each place above has its own.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Falling limbs, flood, fire and the crocodile are the camp's four killers; the old camp sites answered all four [ref:wiki-camaldulensis] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:crocwise].
- A grass fire in the late dry runs faster than a person [ref:pbg-cape-york].
- Blinding smoke from the milky-sapped trees [ref:anderson1996].
- Native title covers camping on country for the holders [ref:alrc].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Camping rules, closures and native title differ from place to place: see each place above, and ask the Traditional Owners before you camp on their country.

locations.summary: Camping in the Hann's country is recorded three ways: Roth's sleeping platforms and palm-leaf huts in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay about 1900 [ref:roth1910-huts]; the camps of the Kuku Thaypan Elders, recorded by Standley, whose thesis is named for the campfire [ref:standley2019]; and Rinyirru's rules for campers today [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

sections.heading: How people camped here
sections.body:
**Many fires.** The anthropologist Donald Thomson, travelling in 1928–33, 'had noted seeing fire on the landscape in Kuku Thaypan country for camping at night and had remarked on the number of fires in one group camping, some were families; some were separate camps for women and men, others for Elders with family groups' [ref:standley2019].

**The Elders' camps.** Camping with Kuku Thaypan Elder Dr Tommy George, Standley found 'our camps were of circular nature', with the visitor placed away from the outer edge, 'not closest to the edge of the lagoon'; those lagoons 'can and do contain large saltwater crocodiles'. Her job was to see 'that the fire was stoked before I retired to bed and that there was enough good dry wood to stoke the campfire easily available nearby' [ref:standley2019]. The Elders say some lagoons were once kept free of saltwater crocodiles, 'actively netted out of places where people had regular camps for safety' [ref:standley2019]. Boxwood 'burns hot and makes good coals for fire and cooking' [ref:standley2019].

**Around the fire.** The thesis takes its name from 'sitting around a campfire on country, relaxed, listening to the Elders and family members telling and re-living experiences of country, sharing and re-affirming knowledge' [ref:standley2019].

**Roth's huts and platforms (about 1900)** [ref:roth1910-huts]:

- **Sleeping platforms**, 'common in the hinterland of Princess Charlotte Bay': a bunk of short sticks across two ridge-poles on forked uprights, five to six feet high, for three or four people, with 'a sheet or two of bark on the cross-pieces'. A fire burns in front, 'the smoke from which keeps the sleepers free from mosquitoes; the fire is never built immediately beneath'. Roth's names: Koko-warra **barpur**, Koko-lamalama **arrianggar**, Koko-rarmul **ngamba**.
- **Dome huts.** On the Kennedy River Roth watched a hut built of cabbage-tree palm leaves (*Livistona*) on a frame of bent withes, the leaves held down by heavy timbers. Around the shores of Princess Charlotte Bay the frame could be 'over a dozen' crossed hoops.

sections.heading: Camping safely here
sections.body: Rinyirru's rules: 'Camp at least 2m above the high water mark and at least 50m from the water's edge. Avoid places where native animals and domestic stock drink. Never leave food scraps, fish frames or bait at a camp site.' 'Mosquito nets are recommended for overnight camping' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body:
**In Rinyirru.** 'Camping permits are required for all camping areas' and 'all camping must be booked prior to arriving'. The park 'is closed throughout the wet season every year': camping areas south of the Lakefield ranger base from 1 December to 31 May, those north of it from 1 December to 30 June [ref:qpws-rinyirru-safe]. 'Do not remove plant material, living or dead' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-about].

**On the Hann.** The upper Hann is the Possum People's country and the middle and lower Hann are Thaypan country, under native title determinations of November 2023 [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan]. The Kuku Thaypan Elders' fire workshops brought people to camp and burn together, and grew until 'more and more campfires were being made at the event and then across the continent'; one, in 2011, was the Hann River Fire Workshop [ref:standley2019].

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the station's camping page and induction add the modern rules: where the river camps are, the fire and firewood rules, the wet-season road closures, and [Crocwise](entry:freshwater-crocodile) at the water [ref:kw-camping] [ref:kw-induction] [ref:crocwise].

sections.heading: Where to camp here
sections.body: On Karma Waters the station's river camps are on the old sandy terraces above the Mitchell [ref:kw-camping] [ref:anderson1996]. The carbeen, the grey boxwood of the firewood list, has two records within 30 km of the homestead [ref:wiki-tessellaris].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body: The roads close in the wet, as the wet always closed the creek beds [ref:kw-camping] [ref:bom-palmerville].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: The station's induction, camping page and fire rules apply [ref:kw-induction] [ref:kw-camping]. Native title covers camping on country for the holders; the station's lease and the campground's rules run alongside it [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The Karma Waters river camps are on the old terraces and the wet closes the roads as it always closed the creek beds; the carbeen and the paperbark are on the bank for the fire [ref:kw-camping] [ref:anderson1996]. The Western Yalanji names for the camps along the Mitchell are for the contribution box below.

locations.summary: Anderson's account of the inland Kuku Yalanji of the Bloomfield is the fullest record of where and when the old people camped: by the freshwater creeks, 'the focal points of economic life for inlanders' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where the old people camped here
sections.body: **The camps by season.** 'In the inland areas around Bloomfield, three types of environment were habitually exploited: upper montane and riverine rainforest, open eucalypt and woodland forests and the freshwater creek systems. The latter were undoubtedly the focal points of economic life for inlanders, where good sandy campsites, shade and proximity to freshwater year-round could be found. Dry season camps were in the sandy beds of the smaller dry creeks or on the sandy terraces above the running creeks. The wet season camps were generally on the ridges between creek gullies, well above flood level, but not too far from water supplies. The pattern of movement in the inland areas was one of short distance shifts within a series of major camps along the creeks. In the dry, the smaller nuclear family-based groups would move out away from the main camping areas and set up temporary "branch" camps in order to exploit non-seasonal opportunistic resources such as eelfish, tortoises, wallabies and goannas. In the wet, the tendency was to contract into larger more permanent camps. Large camps with up to 100 people also existed in the dry during the harvesting and preparation of seasonal, bulk' foods such as the [zamia](entry:zamia) nuts, processed beside 'a shallow, but fast-flowing section of creek' with 'large flat rocks with small indentations in them' [ref:anderson1996].
